response.text:
Short answer: the sender does not see anything different. Archiving vs deleting only affects your copy of the message and how your mail system stores/organizes it — not the sender’s view.

What “archive” typically does
- Removes the message from your Inbox view (or removes the “Inbox” label in Gmail) but keeps the message in your mailbox (often in an “All Mail” or “Archive” folder).
- The message remains searchable and counts against your storage quota.
- If the sender replies later, the new reply will normally appear in your Inbox (or thread) as usual.
- You can restore or re-label the archived message at any time.

What “delete” typically does
- Moves the message to a Trash/Deleted Items folder (or flags it as deleted). It is usually removed from normal folders/labels.
- It may be recoverable for a limited time (e.g., many providers keep messages in Trash for about 30 days) and then is permanently removed.
- Once permanently deleted it is not visible in your mailbox anymore (although the provider may retain backups or logs according to their retention policies).
- Future replies from the sender still arrive normally; deleting your previous copy doesn’t block or notify the sender.

Other notes and exceptions
- Exact behavior varies by provider and by client (Gmail’s label model vs. folder-based systems like some IMAP/Exchange setups). For example, Gmail’s “archive” removes the Inbox label and keeps the message in All Mail; “delete” moves it to Trash for a limited retention period.
- Organizational policies, legal holds, or backup/retention rules can mean “deleted” messages are still retained by the provider or admin.
- If you want a provider-specific description (e.g., Gmail, Outlook, Exchange), tell me which one and I’ll summarize exact behavior and recovery windows.
